scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying data. Disagreement is measured on the wire, not inferred

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. TO RE-EARN: probe the layer this row actually names. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). For cron/realtime/print/cdn the envelope question needs its own instrument and the row should stay owed until one exists, rather than inheriting a reading from whatever service happened to answer.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: every response this page's reads receive carries the envelope shape its client expects
withdrawn_evidence.checked: PASSES. Of this page's 10 read relation(s), 8 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, hive_audit_log, hive_members, inventory_items, inventory_transactions, parts_staged_reservations, project_l).  PLATFORM RESULT: across 40 relations, ZERO envelope defects and ZERO status/body disagreements. The error envelope is well-formed - {code, message, details, hint} on every error body, 400 (not 500) for an unknown column, 406 with PGRST116 for a single-object read of 0 rows, and a Content-Range header whenever Prefer: count=exact is asked. The status always agrees with the body: no 2xx carries an error object and no 4xx omits a machine-readable code. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, asking the oracle's question in the two halves it has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, asking the oracle's question in the two halves it has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed: a page writing two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them, so a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between them leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page writing one table and letting a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic BY CONSTRUCTION, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants checked against live data and ALL HOLD. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ★ROSTER: {"client-sequenced": 11, "single-or-no-write": 11}. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT green even though nothing is broken today. It writes asset_nodes + inventory_items; asset_nodes + inventory_transactions; hive_audit_log + inventory_items and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC writing both - so a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. Every declared invariant holds against live data, which is genuinely reassuring, but 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code; banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. ★RE-WALKED AFTER THIS SESSION'S TWELVE PRODUCT FIXES so the evidence carries digests of the code as it now stands - R4b expired the prior rows because the fixes changed the very functions they rested on. Re-WALKED, never re-baselined.

evidence.asserts: A multi-row or multi-table write either lands whole or not at all; a half-applied write is visible as an inconsistency in the ledger. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - write_atomicity exercises every declared ledger invariant live, inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK, and checks that the paired halves of a write cannot come apart.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every declared ledger invariant holds against the live database, exercised transactionally rather than reasoned about. The exposure the gate reports rather than hides is the honest part: 11 pages sequence TWO writes client-side, which is structural risk (a tab closed between them leaves the second undone) and is recorded as exposure, not counted as a failure, because no half-write has actually occurred in the data. That distinction is the same one this platform learned the hard way from a one-sided ledger write that passed every guard - the difference between "this could come apart" and "this has come apart" decides whether you are hardening a path or repairing rows. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration or function under this claim still expires it, and replay re-earns it in one command instead of a browser session.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed. A page that writes two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them: a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between the two leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page that writes one table and lets a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic by construction, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants were checked against live data and ALL HOLD - the inventory running balance, transactions with no orphan item, every reply and every live safety post carrying its XP award row, no XP row outliving a deleted post unreversed, no staged reservation both consumed and released, one AMC briefing per hive per shift date, a scope item not completed twice, no project child outliving its project. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp, and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ROSTER-WIDE: 11 pages client-sequenced, 11 single-or-no-write. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT banked green even though nothing is broken today. The page writes asset_nodes + inventory_items; asset_nodes + inventory_transactions; hive_audit_log + inventory_items and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC that writes both. So the first clause of the oracle ('either lands whole or not at all') is false as a structural matter: a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. WHAT THE LEDGER SAYS IS THE OTHER HALF, and it is genuinely reassuring rather than decorative: every declared conservation invariant holds against live data, so no half-write has HAPPENED. But 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code - the same shape as a latent null-collapse that no row has triggered. Banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either the second write moves behind a trigger or an RPC (making it atomic by construction, which is what 11 of the 22 pages already do and what the control pair demonstrates), or a probe interrupts the page BETWEEN the two calls and shows the ledger invariant catching the resulting half-state - which would prove the second clause with teeth instead of by absence. ★CORRECTION TO THE STRENGTH OF THIS CLAIM, made after reading what the pairs actually are. The prover enumerates every PAIR OF RELATIONS a page writes and asks whether the database links them - a cartesian over the page's write set, NOT a list of observed co-writes. Most of these pairs are therefore not one logical write split in two: community_posts + community_reactions are two separate user actions, asset_nodes + inventory_items are two different edits, and hive_audit_log pairs with everything because it is appended alongside many actions. A HALF-WRITE IS ONLY POSSIBLE WHERE A SINGLE ACTION WRITES BOTH TABLES, which is a smaller set than the pair count suggests - the plausible ones on this roster are flows where one submit genuinely lands two rows (resume_documents + resume_versions on an upload; logbook + schedule_items when a planned item is completed; asset_nodes + logbook when an asset is created during capture). Which pairs those are cannot be read from pg_trigger; it needs the page's write FUNCTIONS traced. SO THE ROW STAYS OWED FOR A NARROWER REASON THAN THE PAIR COUNT IMPLIES: the page writes multiple tables with no DB linkage, which MAY permit a half-write on whichever action writes two - and the ledger shows none has occurred. This is not a claim that every listed pair is a live risk, and the distinction is recorded rather than letting a large pair count read as a large defect. CONCRETE NEXT SLICE: not 'add triggers', but trace this page's write functions, identify which single actions write two tables, and interrupt only those between the calls.

findings.detail: SILENT AT ALL FIVE SAMPLES - inventory never tells the reader anything failed, and affirmatively certifies the opposite. Healthy: 27 parts, 3 low. Under an injected 500 on its own reads: every figure 0, and the page renders 'No parts in inventory yet - Click Add Part to register your first spare', 'OUT OF STOCK 0 - No parts at zero qty - CLEAR', 'LOW STOCK 0 - Every part above its reorder point - STOCKED', 'PENDING PARTS 0 - Nothing awaiting supervisor sign-off - CLEAR', and 'WHAT TO DO NEXT: No parts registered.' It also stamps 'Live - refreshed on load - Based on your inventory & stock movements', a freshness claim that is false at the instant it is made. Body text drops 1858 -> 1020 chars: the real content is gone and nothing replaces it but reassurance. NO NOTICE AT ANY OF 1.2s / 3s / 5s / 9s / 15s - unlike logbook (notice at 1.2s only) and pm-scheduler (notice at all five, same lens, same run). inventory.html's single 'Check your connection' string sits on a WRITE path, not on this read, so there is nothing here to be transient about: this is silence, not a dismissed toast. CONSEQUENCE IN THE FIELD: a stockroom that answers 'STOCKED - every part above its reorder point' while it is blind. Someone reorders what is already on the shelf, or skips a job for a part that was in stock. Of the three pages measured this is the only one where the reader is given no signal whatsoever. FIX (batched per A15; already proven on platform-actions.html:591/615 this session): sentinel the figures on _error instead of defaulting to 0, AND suppress the CLEAR / STOCKED verdict words, because a verdict computed from an unarrived count must not render at all - not even as a zero. || METHOD: MEASURED AS A TIMELINE, NOT A SNAPSHOT, and that is the whole point of the reading. A 500 is injected into the page's own reads (fetch wrapped before load; /auth/v1/ deliberately NOT blocked so the identity guard can still read a valid session), the interception is COUNTED and a verdict over zero interceptions is refused as vacuous, and then the surface is sampled five times across ~15s rather than once. WHY THE TIMELINE MATTERS: a single-instant reading of this oracle is not reproducible, and this bank holds the receipts in both directions. An earlier pass recorded 'says nothing on failure' across 11 of 16 pages and then RETRACTED it, because that lens was <main>-scoped and missed a body-level notice; a later pass recorded all four CC oracles passing on 12 of 12. Sampling over time shows BOTH WERE TRUE AT DIFFERENT INSTANTS - the failure notice is a toast that auto-dismisses while the zeros it was explaining stay on screen indefinitely. So 'did the page speak?' is the wrong question, and 'is the reader who arrives three seconds late still told?' is the right one. POSITIVE CONTROL in the same run: the identical lens caught pm-scheduler's notice at all five samples, so a silent reading is the page's silence and not the lens's blindness - which is the check the retracted finding lacked.

findings.title: the verdict and heroes are fixed and were measured correctly, but three stat pills still read 0 under a 500 - a surface the original evidence never examined
findings.detail:
WHAT THE GREEN CLAIMED AND STILL PROVES. That a server fault says something failed without blaming the session and without rendering an empty result as though answered. Its value_checked names exactly what it measured: heroes dashed to '- - -' / UNKNOWN, the verdict 'Could not load your inventory', and the ABSENCE of CLEAR|STOCKED|'No parts in inventory yet', persisting at 12s. Re-measured today under a fresh guarded 500 injection, ALL THREE of those still hold: the page renders 'Could not load your inventory - Stock levels are unknown right now, not zero. Check your connection and reload before ordering or issuing parts.' and inv-out-hero, inv-low-hero and inv-pending-hero all read a dash. That fix works and this withdrawal does not take it back.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT DID NOT COVER. The lens looked at the hero tiles and the verdict wording. It never enumerated the stat pills. With 5 reads answered 500, today's guarded reading shows stat-total=0, stat-low=0 and stat-out=0 VISIBLE on the same view, at the same moment as the sentence saying stock levels are unknown and not zero.

WHY THAT FALSIFIES THE ASSERTION RATHER THAN MERELY EXTENDING IT. The row asserts the page does not render an empty result as though the server had honestly answered. Three pills reading 0 are exactly that. The screen now contradicts itself: the prose says 'unknown right now, not zero' while three numbers say zero. A careful reader trusts the sentence; a reader glancing at a phone in a plant reads the pills. Leaving this green would tell a future session that inventory handles a 500 honestly, when three numbers on that view still assert a stock position the server never gave.

THIS IS THE lens-measured-a-fraction-of-the-page CLASS, and the sibling rows show the same shape: dayplanner's fixed verdict sits beside an open-items panel still reading '0 open items from Logbook' and 'No open items'; pm-scheduler's sits beside 'No assets yet - Tap the + button'. One fix, three pages, one surface missed on each.

TO RE-EARN: extend the existing _invReadFailed guard to stat-total / stat-low / stat-out so they dash with the heroes, then re-walk with the same guarded window.fetch 500 injection. The fix is the same conditional already in renderInventorySummary - it simply does not reach these three elements.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: a server fault says something failed, without blaming the reader's session and without rendering an empty result as though the server had honestly answered none
withdrawn_evidence.checked: FIXED FIRST, THEN BANKED (A12), AND THE FIX IS VERIFIED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS - a failure oracle that only checks the failure path can be satisfied by a page that is broken all the time. WHAT WAS WRONG, MEASURED: with a 500 injected into this page's own reads (2 interceptions, counted, so the reading is not vacuous), inventory rendered six zeros and told the reader everything was fine - 'OUT OF STOCK 0 / No parts at zero qty / CLEAR', 'LOW STOCK 0 / Every part above its reorder point / STOCKED', 'PENDING PARTS 0 / Nothing awaiting supervisor sign-off / CLEAR', plus 'No parts in inventory yet - click Add Part to register your first spare' and the chip 'Live - refreshed on load'. Healthy, the same page shows 27 parts and 3 low. NO NOTICE APPEARED AT ANY OF FIVE SAMPLES ACROSS ~15s, so this was not a toast that dismissed before I looked: the page was silent, and the words on screen were an affirmative all-clear computed from a count that never arrived. A stockroom that answers STOCKED while blind sends someone to reorder what is on the shelf, or to skip a job for a part that was in stock. THE DIAGNOSIS IS WHY THE FIX IS SMALL: the page ALREADY KNEW. inventory.html:2065 has computed _invReadErr since the P2 'honest-degraded' change, and its own comment says the point is that a transient read failure must not '(b) render as a fake-empty inventory' - but the value was only ever used to write a console warning and to skip the localStorage re-migration. It never reached the render. So this was not a missing detection, it was a detection that stopped one function short of the surface. THE FIX (three edits, no call-site or signature changes): a module-scoped _invReadFailed set from _invReadErr at the load site; a guard at the top of renderInventorySummary that renders the em-dash sentinel with tag UNKNOWN on all three cards, sets the verdict to 'Could not load your inventory - stock levels are unknown right now, not zero. Check your connection and reload before ordering or issuing parts', clears the progress strip and returns before any verdict word can be computed; and a branch in the zero-items list path so #empty-state ('No parts in inventory yet') stays hidden and a 'Could not load your parts - this is a connection problem, not an empty inventory' panel renders instead. The em-dash sentinel matches the fix already proven on platform-actions.html:591/615 in this same session. VERIFIED, SICK: heroes '- - -', tags UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN/UNKNOWN, verdict 'Could not load your inventory', #empty-state not visible, no CLEAR / STOCKED / 'above its reorder point' / 'No parts at zero qty' anywhere in the body, no 'No parts in inventory yet', and zero uncaught JS errors. VERIFIED, HEALTHY (the control that stops a broken-always page passing): heroes '0 3 0', verdict '2 parts critically low', 8 rows rendered, no failure wording, no JS errors. The healthy page still says CLEAR for out-of-stock, which is CORRECT - a genuine zero is a real all-clear, and the oracle is about a zero that was never measured, not about the digit. AND IT IS PERMANENT, NOT TRANSIENT, which is the distinction the timeline sampling in this cohort established: the failure lives in the rendered STATE, so it was still on screen at 12s. Pages that delegate this to a toast (logbook, project-manager) tell the reader once for about a second and then show confident zeros forever; those rows are qualified rather than green for exactly that reason.

findings.title: NOT BANKED - fail_401: an expired session is not surfaced honestly on this page. THIS FAILS ON 17 OF 17 PAGES WALKED, and the fix is ADOPTION, not a new message
findings.detail: FAILURE STATES ARE INJECTED, never waited for. failures() intercepts the page's own reads and answers them with the failure under test, then reads what the page TELLS A PERSON. Every mutating verb is answered by a stub rather than forwarded - decided by blockWrite across the WHOLE Supabase surface, rpc and edge functions included - so nothing reaches the shared test database. The path is verified unchanged across the injection, and the surface is asserted before it: an expired session earlier today made 19 of 22 pages return identical landing-page readings, and 3 pages were REFUSED by that guard on this very sweep rather than measured. The navigation fence held on 16 of 16 pages read. THE ORACLE IS WHAT THE READER IS TOLD, not whether an error was caught. A caught error that renders nothing is indistinguishable, from the reader's side, from success. Stamped ::v=3: the top-level digest is a SET of per-statement content hashes, so a shared-library append expires nothing while a modify or delete correctly expires. Self-tested 8/8. FINDING: Injecting a 401 into this page's reads, the page does not tell the reader their session expired, does not name the session as the cause, and does not state the consequence for what they were doing. THE REFLEX IS TO WRITE THE MISSING MESSAGE AND THAT WOULD BE WRONG - it already exists. utils.js:1568 reads 'Your session expired, so nothing was saved. Sign in again and redo this step.' and :1611 has the read equivalent, with _WH_PG_DENIAL at :1518 and a careful 401-versus-403 note beneath it. There is even a comment recording that this was fixed once on the inquiry path, where a 42501 told a SIGNED-IN buyer their session had expired, and that 'the shared helper kept the bug for every other path'. Writing a new string would add a second source of truth for text that is already correct. SO THE DEFECT IS ADOPTION: the read path catches the status and never renders whReadError's text. A uniform 17-of-17 failure is not seventeen independent lapses, it is one shared path swallowing the status - which means ONE fix earns all seventeen rows in a single sweep. Same shape as the other platform-wide finds in this arc: ::placeholder absent everywhere, companion-launcher.js with no prefers-reduced-motion block at all. AND THE PROBE IS NOT AT FAULT, which matters before acting on a 17/17 result: fail_null_field passes on 16 of 16 pages under the same injection harness. A broken probe does not pass one injection everywhere and fail another everywhere. Row stays owed; measure adoption at the point of RENDER, not by the helper's existence.

findings.title: RETRACTED - the fail_timeout failure I recorded here was MY main-scoped text read missing a body-level notice, not a defect on this page
findings.detail: RETRACTED - THIS WAS MY INSTRUMENT, NOT THIS PAGE. I recorded fail_timeout failing on 11 of 16 pages and fail_partial on 13 of 16, described them as pages that say nothing on a timeout and present a partial result as complete, and wrote per-page findings saying so. All four CC oracles now pass on 12 of 12 pages, and NOTHING was changed on any timeout or partial code path in between. What changed is the PROBE: its text scope was document.querySelector('main'), and these pages render their failure messages into toasts, banners and live regions - which are fixed-position and therefore direct children of <body>, because a fixed element inside a transformed or overflow-clipped ancestor positions against that ancestor instead of the viewport. main.innerText could never contain them. So the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf. HOW I FOUND IT, and why it is worth recording rather than quietly re-banking: I added a central 401 notice at getDb()'s transport seam, VERIFIED it rendering - the element was in the DOM carrying the text - and fail_401 still read every sub-assertion false. That contradiction is what exposed the scope bug. The failure oracle now reads main PLUS live/alert/notice containers, deduped, and deliberately NOT all of body, because nav and hub chrome carry standing words like 'offline' and 'retry' that would forge a pass on every page. WHAT SURVIVES: the fail_401 finding was REAL. Before the central fix there was no session notice on any page at all - no element existed to be missed - so 12 of 12 pages genuinely told a reader nothing when their session died, and the fix at getDb() is what created the notice they now show. That one is not withdrawn. Only the timeout and partial claims are, and they are withdrawn in full. THE LESSON IS THE ONE THIS ARC KEEPS RE-LEARNING: an instrument that measures the wrong REGION produces well-formed readings, and a uniform failure across many pages should raise suspicion of the probe before it is written up as a platform defect. The same lens-scope error once measured 15 of 518 nodes for contrast because it scoped to <main> while the report mounted outside it.

findings.title: RETRACTION SUPERSEDED - the withdrawal above rested on a contaminated reading; fail_partial genuinely FAILS here (9 of 12 pages), reinstated
findings.detail: THE RETRACTION ON THIS ROW WAS ITSELF WRONG, and this note supersedes it. Three measurements of fail_partial exist and only the middle one is contaminated: (1) FIRST READ, text scope = <main>: failed on 13 of 16 pages. (2) SECOND READ, after I widened the scope to include body-level notice regions: passed on 12 of 12 - and on the strength of that I retracted the finding on 12 pages, writing that 'the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf'. (3) THIRD READ, after I made my own 401 notice CLEAR ITSELF: fails on 9 of 12. NOTHING ON ANY PARTIAL CODE PATH CHANGED ACROSS THOSE THREE. What changed in (2) is that the central session notice I had just added to getDb() was still pinned to the page from the 401 injection earlier in the same failures() run, so namesTheFailure was matching MY OWN leftover text - 'Your session expired, so this page could not be loaded' - rather than anything the page said about a truncated payload. Reading (1) and reading (3) AGREE with each other; (2) is the outlier, and (2) is the one I acted on. SO THE ORIGINAL FINDING STANDS, at 9 of 12 rather than 13 of 16: on this page a truncated payload is rendered without the reader being told part of the data is missing. The withdrawal note above should be read as evidence about my instrument's history, not as an exoneration of this page. WHY THIS HAPPENED, because the mechanism matters more than the count: I fixed one artefact (a main-scoped text read) and in the same window introduced another (a notice that outlived its injection), then used a measurement taken between the two to overturn a finding. A correction is only as good as the reading behind it, and a reading taken while another fix is half-landed is not a baseline. The rule I keep re-deriving: change ONE thing, re-measure, and never let a retraction rest on a single run - especially not one that flips a uniform FAIL into a uniform PASS, which is the same too-good-to-be-true signature that should raise suspicion of the instrument in either direction.

findings.detail: FAILS, AND IT FAILS THROUGH THE FIX I LANDED EARLIER TODAY - recorded against my own work rather than left for someone else to trip over. The fail_500 fix on this page routes a failed read into the rendered STATE (an em-dash sentinel, tag UNKNOWN, a verdict that names the failure) and it is verified for that case. OFFLINE IS A DIFFERENT FAILURE MODE AND IT IS NOT COVERED. MEASURED: fetch was made to REJECT (Promise.reject(new TypeError('Failed to fetch'))) for every /rest/v1/, /functions/v1/ and /rpc/ request while leaving /auth/v1/ alive, with navigator.onLine forced false - i.e. a real no-network condition rather than a server answering badly. 13-19 requests blocked per page, so the perturbation is not marginal. Result on all four pages measured (inventory, dayplanner, pm-scheduler, logbook): every KPI reads **0**, ZERO sentinels rendered, and the verdict is frozen at its initial placeholder - 'Computing stock health...', 'Loading day plan...', 'Computing PM compliance...' - which will never resolve. inventory additionally still shows CLEAR / STOCKED wording. THE ROOT, PRECISELY: my flags are set from `res.error` - a RESOLVED response carrying an error body. A rejected promise never produces one, so the flag stays false and the guard I added never runs; worse, the rejection propagates and aborts the init chain before the summary renders at all, which is why the verdict keeps its HTML placeholder instead of even reaching the zero branch. A 500 and a dead network arrive through two different doors and I only instrumented one. THIS IS ALSO THE STUCK-PLACEHOLDER SHAPE the same session found on skillmatrix (a persistent, correct failure toast beside a verdict reading 'Computing skill progress...' forever): nothing false is ASSERTED by a frozen 'Computing...', so an oracle hunting fabricated values passes it while a person watches a spinner that will never finish. Here it is worse, because the KPIs underneath it read 0. A toast does say 'check your connection' on these pages, so the reader is not told nothing - but the same timing evidence from this session applies: toasts on these pages fire within 150-240ms and dismiss, while the zeros persist indefinitely. TO FINISH (batched per A15, one wave, no mid-walk edits): set the same _<x>ReadFailed flag in the CATCH block each of these load functions already has (inventory.html:2214 'inventory load failed', and the equivalents on the other three), and CALL the summary renderer from that catch so the sentinel path runs even when the load threw. RETRACTION OF MY OWN PREVIOUS NOTE ON THIS ROW. I wrote that the part-create path writes qty_on_hand with no paired transaction and called it a product defect. findings.detail: This row is green and stays green, and the measurement that supports it is worth naming precisely, because the obvious version of this check FAILS and the failure is not a bug. MEASURED TWO WAYS. (1) The ledger's own running balance is perfect: for all 81 parts, the most recent transaction's qty_after equals the part's current qty_on_hand - 0 disagreements. That is conservation in the sense that matters: no movement is lost, and the chain from the last recorded movement to the current stock figure is intact. (2) But sum(qty_change) over all of a part's transactions equals qty_on_hand for only 16 of 81 parts - 65 disagree, worst gap 205 units. THOSE TWO FACTS TOGETHER ARE THE EXPLANATION, NOT A CONTRADICTION: if movements were being dropped, the qty_after chain could not stay consistent. Parts were created with an OPENING BALANCE that was never written as a transaction, so the log records movements SINCE stocking rather than the whole history from zero. WHAT IT COSTS ANYWAY, and why it is recorded rather than waved through: an auditor cannot reconstruct current stock from the transaction log alone - they must trust qty_on_hand as a starting fact. For a stockroom that is a real limitation: 'where did these 205 units come from' has no answer in the ledger. The fix is one opening-balance transaction per part at creation (type 'opening', qty_change = initial quantity), after which sum(qty_change) becomes a genuine independent check instead of an approximation.

MEASURED: parts_staged_reservations holds **1** row whose item_id points at no surviving inventory_items row. WHAT AN ORPHAN RESERVATION DOES: a staged reservation exists to HOLD stock for a job, and available stock is on-hand minus reservations. A hold against a part that no longer exists cannot be released by closing or cancelling the job that created it, because the release path resolves through the item. So it is a permanent silent subtraction if any 'available' figure joins through it, and a permanently unreleasable row if not. One row is not an emergency, but it proves the release/cleanup path has a gap rather than merely being untested - and the count only goes up. TO FINISH: find how the item was deleted while a reservation survived (a delete that does not cascade or release is the likely cause), then either cascade the release on item delete or add a reconciliation that releases holds whose item is gone. Also worth a NOT NULL foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE or RESTRICT so the database refuses the state instead of tolerating it.

evidence.asserts: this page's severity and state words mean the same thing they mean on every other surface - one vocabulary, no per-page synonym for the same rung
evidence.checked: MEASURED BY HARVESTING THE WORDS EACH PAGE ACTUALLY SHOWS A READER AND COMPARING THEM ACROSS PAGES - this oracle is inherently cross-surface, so it cannot be settled from one page. Eight production surfaces were loaded in one authenticated pass (identity and pathname guarded on each) and every rendered leaf whose whole text is a severity or state term was collected. THE OBSERVED PLATFORM VOCABULARY: alert-hub CLEAR/CRITICAL/HIGH; pm-scheduler CRITICAL/LOW/MEDIUM plus DUE SOON/ON TRACK/OVERDUE; inventory CLEAR/LOW; hive WARNING plus CLOSED; dayplanner OPEN/OVERDUE; logbook OPEN; project-manager ACTIVE/NONE. WHAT THAT ESTABLISHES, AND IT IS THE ABSENCE OF A SYNONYM RATHER THAN THE PRESENCE OF A LIST: (1) severity is ONE LADDER - CRITICAL / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW - shared by alert-hub and pm-scheduler, with NO competing synonym anywhere in the pass (no URGENT, no SEVERE, no P1, no ordinal like 'level 3'). Two pages using a different word for the same rung is exactly the drift this oracle exists to catch, and it does not occur. (2) CLEAR means 'nothing wrong' on BOTH pages that use it (alert-hub, inventory). (3) OVERDUE means past its due date on BOTH pm-scheduler and dayplanner. (4) OPEN means not-yet-closed on BOTH logbook and dayplanner, and hive's CLOSED is its complement rather than a rival term. WHY A SYNONYM WOULD MATTER MORE THAN A MISSING WORD: a technician who learns that CRITICAL is the top rung on the alert inbox must be able to carry that meaning to the PM scheduler. A second vocabulary does not merely look untidy - it silently rescales urgency between two screens the same person uses in one shift. SCOPE, STATED HONESTLY: the default view of each page, signed in, at 1000px. Terms that only appear inside modals or after a state change are not in this denominator and belong to the V2/V3 rows. analytics rendered NO severity or state term in its default view and is therefore left OWED rather than credited with a pass - a page with nothing to check is not a page that checks out. THIS PAGE CONTRIBUTED: severity CLEAR / LOW - every term of which is used identically on the other surfaces that display it.

evidence.asserts: every quantity a reader could act on carries its unit; a bare number is either a count of things or prints its own denominator
evidence.checked: SETTLED BY READING EVERY FLAGGED FIGURE INDIVIDUALLY, after TWO generations of automated classifier both failed - which is why this row rests on inspection with a stated denominator rather than on a lens verdict. GEN-1 FAILED FIVE WAYS and was discarded: it flagged wizard STEP ORDINALS (1 2 3) as unit-less quantities; it lacked bare 'h' and 'year' in its vocabulary, so analytics' CORRECT 6.2h MTTR and 1-year window were called bare; it flagged BOUNDED SCORES that print their own denominator (hive readiness 62/100); and its fixed 3-level ancestor walk escaped the label region entirely, returning the PAGE TITLE as a figure's context on dayplanner. GEN-2 walks up only until a label-bearing ancestor is found and ABSTAINS when none exists (24 abstentions on dayplanner, 21 on analytics), exempts ordinals and printed-denominator scores, and widened the unit vocabulary. THEN EVERY REMAINING FLAG WAS READ BY HAND and confirmed dimensionless: '30 machines', '3 low' / '0 out', hive readiness sub-scores 100/42/70, 'Mechanical - 3 +' skill level, and per-asset failure counts (CR-001 11, GEN-001 10). THE REASON NO LENS CAN CLOSE THIS ORACLE: 'is this number dimensionless?' is a judgement about the DOMAIN, not a lexical property of the label. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. Its failure messaging is otherwise good - 'Could not load your inventory - Stock levels are unknown right now, not zero. Check your connection and reload before ordering or issuing parts.' with `inv-out-hero`, `inv-low-hero` and `inv-pending-hero` all dashed - which makes the absent retry the remaining gap: the page correctly tells the reader to reload, because it cannot offer to retry. SO A READER'S ONLY RECOURSE IS A FULL PAGE RELOAD, which on a phone in a plant means losing whatever was on screen and paying the whole load again on the connection that just failed. THE PLATFORM HAS THE PATTERN ALREADY, so this is unadopted rather than undesigned: community renders a toast reading 'Couldn't load the community feed. Check your connection and try again.' with a **Retry** button beside it, and public-feed's Retry was measured firing a real re-request and then rendering 15 posts. Six of the seven pages measured in this sweep have neither. WHAT WOULD PASS IT: a control that re-issues the failed read and is measurable as such - the probe counts requests fired after the click, so a button that merely re-renders the previous failure fails too. That distinction is not hypothetical: it is the exact defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed. MEASURED BY FAILING EVERY READ AT window.fetch AND COUNTING WHAT THE PAGE DOES NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request is answered with a synthetic 500 (`{"code":"500"}`, Content-Type application/json) while `/auth/v1/` is left untouched so the session survives - so the page sees a server fault, not a dead network, and supabase-js resolves it into an error object exactly as PostgREST would. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. THE INJECTION HAD TO MOVE FROM THE TRANSPORT TO window.fetch, AND THAT MATTERS FOR TRUST. An earlier pass used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered real data - a registered service worker sits between the page and the transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. Every verdict from that pass would have been false, and the interception counter is the only reason it was caught rather than banked. AND THE READING IS GUARDED INSIDE THE EVALUATE: it refuses unless the auth token holds the expected uid, `location.pathname` still ends in this page's own file, and the body is NOT in the 13,000-16,000 char landing-page band. A previous unguarded pass returned byte-identical output for seven different pages - 14,677 chars of marketing copy - because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. Seven page-specific verdicts, all of them the landing page. The guard is not ceremony.

findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. findings.title: FAILS THE FIRST CLAUSE ONLY, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE FINDING. The oracle: 'when the primary is down the fallback engages and the surface says which it used, rather than pretending nothing happened.' Two clauses, and this page is measured against both. MEASURED with 5 reads answered 500: this page
findings.detail: FAILS THE FIRST CLAUSE ONLY, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE FINDING. The oracle: 'when the primary is down the fallback engages and the surface says which it used, rather than pretending nothing happened.' Two clauses, and this page is measured against both. MEASURED with 5 reads answered 500: this page DOES say the primary is down, in domain language - **'Could not load your inventory - Stock levels are unknown right now, not zero. Check your connection and reload before ordering or issuing parts.'** - and it dashes its tiles rather than zeroing them (`inv-out-hero`, `inv-low-hero` and `inv-pending-hero` all read a dash). So it does not pretend nothing happened, and that half is genuinely done. WHAT IS MISSING IS THE FALLBACK ITSELF, and no page-level fix can supply it: THERE IS NO READ FALLBACK ON THIS PLATFORM, AND THAT IS PROVEN FROM THE SERVICE WORKER'S SOURCE RATHER THAN INFERRED. `sw.js` handles API traffic in one branch - `if (url.includes('supabase.co') || url.includes('fonts.goog') ...) e.respondWith(fetch(e.request).catch(() => new Response('', { status: 503 })))` (sw.js:195-200) - so a failed read resolves to an EMPTY 503 body. And `cache.put` appears **nowhere in the file**, so no API response is ever stored: `caches.match()` cannot hit for a `/rest/v1/` URL because nothing put one there. The 26-entry `SHELL_FILES` precache holds HTML, CSS and JS only. SO THE FIRST CLAUSE CANNOT BE SATISFIED FOR READS BY CONSTRUCTION - there is nothing to engage. The offline layer this platform does have is for WRITES (the `wh_logbook_offline` / `wh_dayplanner_offline` / `wh_assethub_offline` IndexedDB queues), which is a different oracle. That makes the second clause the whole test: does the surface say the primary is down, or does it pretend nothing happened? SO THIS ROW IS NOT A PAGE DEFECT BUT A PLATFORM GAP, recorded here because the oracle asks for a fallback and there is none to engage. It is banked as a finding rather than a pass so the debt stays visible, and rather than `declared-na` because the subject is real - the platform HAS an offline layer, it just serves writes only. NOTE, recorded on this page's fail_500 row rather than repeated here: three `stat-*` pills still read 0 under the same failure, contradicting the sentence beside them. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: cache the last successful read per surface (an IndexedDB mirror beside the existing write queues, or a `cache.put` on the API branch keyed by query) and label the rendered copy with its age - 'showing your last synced copy from 14:20'. That is one central mechanism, not 22 page fixes, which is the CENTRALIZE-FIRST call. MEASURED TWO INDEPENDENT WAYS, so the reading does not rest on one injection style. (1) Every `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request answered with a synthetic 500 at `window.fetch`, `/auth/v1/` left alone so the session survives, interceptions counted and a zero-interception run refused as vacuous. (2) A genuine `setOffline(true)` navigation with the service-worker cache WARM. THE SECOND METHOD TOOK THREE ATTEMPTS TO GET HONEST, WHICH IS WHY IT IS TRUSTWORTHY NOW. Navigating to `/workhive/logbook.html` offline served the branded offline shell every time - not because the page is unavailable offline, but because `SHELL_FILES` precaches ROOT paths (`/logbook.html`) and the `/workhive/` prefix is a different cache key. Measured at the path the cache actually holds, the real page is served. A verdict from the prefixed path would have described a cache miss and called it product behaviour. findings.detail: RECORDED OWED WITH A MIXED IN-FLIGHT READING - not passed, not failed, because the evidence genuinely points both ways and one more measurement decides it. With reads held in flight this page shows explicit loading vocabulary AND 3 dash sentinels (so part of the surface sentinels correctly), while 6 bare numbers are on screen, 6 of them zeros. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER THOSE ZEROS ARE ASSERTIONS OR STATIC HTML DEFAULTS. The KPI heroes ship as `0` in the markup and are overwritten when data lands, so a zero seen mid-load may be untouched initial markup rather than a computed claim - and from outside the two are indistinguishable. dayplanner in this same pass showed 3 in-flight zeros against 2 settled zeros, i.e. its zeros were mostly REAL values, which is exactly why a count alone cannot decide. TO FINISH - one targeted probe, no guesswork: snapshot each KPI element's textContent before the reads resolve and again after, and compare against that element's value in the static HTML. A zero that never changes and equals the markup default is a placeholder; a zero written by the render is a fabricated answer. MEASURED BY DELAYING THE PAGE'S OWN READS, NOT BY GUESSING AT A SLOW NETWORK. Every /rest/v1/ and /rpc/ request is wrapped in a 6-second delay before being forwarded to the real fetch (auth left untouched so the identity guard still works), and the surface is read at 2.2s - i.e. WHILE the reads are provably still in flight. Interceptions are COUNTED and a verdict over zero is refused as vacuous. THE ORACLE IS WHETHER A SLOW READ IS SHOWN AS SLOW rather than answered with a fabricated value, so the in-flight state IS the measurement. Three positive signals are collected independently - skeleton/shimmer/aria-busy elements, explicit loading vocabulary in the body, and dash sentinels - alongside the two things that would betray it: how many bare numbers are on screen, and whether any false-empty sentence has appeared. AN HONEST INSTRUMENT LIMIT, RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the post-delay sample taken 7s later was still MID-LOAD on three pages (skeletons still present), because 6s per read across sequential reads exceeds that wait. So the settled comparison is NOT used for any verdict here - only the in-flight reading. Using a still-loading sample as the 'after' picture would have made every page look permanently broken.

findings.title: the numeric-write lens was blind to a TEXTUAL assertion: inventory renders 'No parts in inventory yet' while its 5 reads are still pending
findings.detail:
WHAT THE GREEN CLAIMED. That inventory never answers with a value it does not have yet, on the strength of a MutationObserver measuring 0 numeric writes before any read resolved - the KPI zeros were static markup, not computed claims. That measurement stands and was correct as far as it went.

WHAT IT MISSED. The lens counted only mutations whose text was purely NUMERIC, so it could not see a sentence. Re-measured with a composed-visibility check (getClientRects + checkVisibility + an ancestor walk for display/visibility/opacity) across 20 pages while reads were held in flight, inventory renders '#empty-state' VISIBLE at top=1075, h=288: 'No parts in inventory yet. Add your first spare part to start monitoring stock levels.' - with 5 reads pending, 0 resolved, and ZERO loading affordances anywhere on the page. The hive holds 27 parts.

WHY THAT IS THE SAME DEFECT THE ORACLE FORBIDS. 'No parts in inventory yet' is an answer, and it is an answer the page does not have yet - the strongest form of the fault, because it is not an ambiguous 0 but a sentence about an empty store-room, addressed to someone deciding whether to order a part. It is the defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed ('pressing Retry answered No public posts yet on a feed with 15 posts'), in a different page.

THE INSTRUMENT DISCRIMINATES, SO THIS IS A PROPERTY OF THE PAGE. Of 20 pages measured the same way, 17 assert nothing while loading; only logbook, inventory and report-sender do. logbook and report-sender already carry slow_honest failures, so inventory was the only green resting on the blind spot.

NOT COVERED BY THE fail_500 FIX EARLIER THIS SESSION. That work added _invReadFailed and keeps #empty-state hidden on the ERROR path, rendering a 'connection problem, not an empty inventory' panel instead. This is the PENDING path - before any read resolves or fails - which that branch never reaches.

TO RE-EARN: keep #empty-state hidden until the items read RESOLVES (a third state beside loaded-and-empty and failed), then re-walk with the same delayed-read probe. alert-hub's dash-plus-Loading idiom and analytics' '- Loading... -' are the in-repo references.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: a slow read is shown as slow - the page never answers with a value it does not have yet
withdrawn_evidence.checked: SETTLED BY WATCHING FOR THE WRITE, WHICH IS THE ONLY THING THAT DISTINGUISHES THE TWO CASES. This row was first recorded owed with a MIXED reading: with reads held in flight the page showed loading vocabulary AND dash sentinels AND bare zeros, and a zero on screen is ambiguous by inspection - every one of these KPI elements SHIPS AS `0` in the static markup (verified by reading the HTML: inv-out/low/pending-hero, stat-overdue/duesoon/ontrack and dp-today/week/overdue-hero are all literal `0`), so a mid-load zero is either untouched markup or a computed claim, and they look identical. THE DECIDING INSTRUMENT: a MutationObserver installed on each KPI element BEFORE page load, with every mutation stamped by how many of the delayed reads had resolved at that instant. Reads are wrapped in a 5s delay and counted on resolution, so 'was this element written while the data was still pending?' becomes a measured fact rather than an inference. MEASURED ON THIS PAGE: 6 reads in flight, **0 resolved**, KPI values read `0,0,0` - and **writesBeforeAnyReadResolved = 0**. The render did not touch those elements at all during the wait. After the reads resolved the render wrote exactly **3** times and the values became `0,3,0` - matching the healthy page (27 parts, 3 low). So the writes happen, and they happen only after the data lands. SO THE ZEROS ARE PLACEHOLDERS, NOT ASSERTIONS, and this oracle passes: the page does not answer with a value it does not have yet. I had expected the opposite - the mixed reading looked like the fabricated-zero shape that this bank has found repeatedly - and the measurement says otherwise. WHAT WOULD HAVE MADE IT FAIL, stated so the pass is falsifiable: any write logged with readsResolvedAtWrite === 0, i.e. the render stamping a count onto a KPI before the data arrived. That is precisely how the fail_500 defect on inventory behaved one state earlier (six zeros under the words CLEAR and STOCKED), so the instrument is known to fire when the fault is real. A REMAINING GAP THIS DOES NOT CLOSE: a static `0` is still a poor placeholder for a reader - it is indistinguishable from a measured zero to anyone looking at the screen, which is why alert-hub's approach (6 skeleton elements and ZERO bare numbers during the wait) is the better pattern on this platform. This row asserts that nothing is FABRICATED, not that the placeholder is ideal.

findings.title: LEFT OWED BECAUSE THIS VIEW'S WRITE IS QUEUE-CLASS AND THE ORACLE AS WORDED DOES NOT DESCRIBE IT - the same finding as logbook, and on this page it is sharper, because ONE page demonstrates BOTH classes.
findings.detail: LEFT OWED BECAUSE THIS VIEW'S WRITE IS QUEUE-CLASS AND THE ORACLE AS WORDED DOES NOT DESCRIBE IT - the same finding as logbook, and on this page it is sharper, because ONE page demonstrates BOTH classes. READ DIRECTLY: the part create/edit path has an offline branch - `if (!navigator.onLine && window._whInvQueue) { await window._whInvQueue.enqueue({ id: item.id, op: 'insert', payload: _row }); showToast('Saved offline, will sync when you reconnect.'); }` - and its own comment states the reasoning: the item is already in the local cache so the worker sees it immediately, and the queue drains on reconnect. That is queue-and-tell, and it is right for a storeman logging a part with no signal. So a green here would credit a refusal that must not exist, and a red would call a working feature a defect. THE SAME PAGE'S DELETE REFUSES, and that split is deliberate rather than inconsistent: confirmDeleteItem was guarded this session with whRequireOnline and is live-proven on V1 (0 inventory_items requests + 'You are offline. Deleting this part needs a connection - nothing was sent, so nothing is half-done.'). Removing the part RECORD is destructive and stock-critical, not field capture, and a queued delete could drain AFTER a concurrent stock movement and take that movement's subject with it. Same table, same page, two classes - which is exactly why the rule is to check for a queue path INSIDE the function rather than to ask whether the page has a queue. ALSO ON THIS PAGE, worth recording so a future walk does not mistake it for a gap: the USE path carries a duplicate-suppression guard (whRecentDuplicate on same item + exact qty + worker + job ref within 15s), because inventory_deduct is atomic but has no idempotency key and a refresh-mid-submit would otherwise double-deduct stock. That is a different oracle again (idempotent_repeat), and it is implemented. WHAT THIS ROW NEEDS INSTEAD: the offline_queued sibling oracle - offline, assert ZERO server writes, the 'Saved offline, will sync when you reconnect.' message, the item visible immediately from the local cache, and then on reconnect that it drains EXACTLY ONCE (the queue is keyed on item.id with op:'insert', so a re-queue replaces rather than duplicates). Eight of the 22 roster pages register queues, so this cell shape is needed roughly a third of the time.

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

findings.title: the part-modal tells you 'No assets registered. Register assets in the Logbook first.' while the assets read is still in flight - and it was banked on a measurement of a different view
findings.detail:
TWO FAULTS, ONE ROW. First, the evidence was IDENTICAL to the V1 row's - a KPI-tile reading of the parts list - so a claim about the part-modal rested on a measurement that never opened it (R7). Second, opening it properly shows the claim is FALSE.

MEASURED. With the fetch wrapper delaying every /rest/v1/ and /rpc/ request, openAddModal() was called at 2.4s with 6 reads in flight and 0 resolved. The modal opened, and '#asset-linker-empty' was VISIBLE (composed-visibility check) reading: 'No assets registered. Register assets in the Logbook first.' No loading vocabulary anywhere in the modal.

THE CODE PATH NAMES ITSELF. renderAssetLinker() at inventory.html:1171-1180 does 'const assets = loadAssets()' and then 'if (assets.length === 0) { linker.innerHTML = ''; linker.appendChild(emptyEl); emptyEl.classList.remove('hidden'); return; }'. There is no third branch for 'not loaded yet', so an unresolved read and a genuinely empty asset register produce the identical screen.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A MISSING SPINNER. The sentence is not merely wrong, it is INSTRUCTIONAL: it sends the user to a different page to register assets that already exist - the hive's assets are read by logbook and asset-hub in the same session. A worker who follows that instruction either creates duplicate asset records or abandons the part they were adding. A dash or a spinner would cost them nothing; this costs them a detour and possibly a duplicate.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

findings.title: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 7 of its 8 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / membe
findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 7 of its 8 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); inventory_items (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 10 read relation(s), 8 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, hive_audit_log, hive_members, inventory_items, inventory_transactions, parts_staged_reservations, project_l).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 7 of its 8 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); inventory_items (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 10 read relation(s), 8 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, hive_audit_log, hive_members, inventory_items, inventory_transactions, parts_staged_reservations, project_l).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.
